Kratom, also known as “mitragynine,” is derived from the Afuragyna speciosa tree native to Southeast Asia. 21, Kratom is an unregulated substance in the United States, and there are no FDA- approved uses for Krator. 22, Although not formally classified as an opiate, kratom contains dozens of psychoactive compounds or alkaloids, many of which are not well understood. While research is ongoing, the two most-studied alkaloids are mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine,oe These CONFIDENTIAL DEF_MOLLER_004334

Like opiates, these compounds can lead to analgesia (release of pain), euphoria, and sedation. 23. Kratom manufacturers and distributors have no reliable basis for specifying the variable doses and potencies of kratom’s various psychoactive compounds in product packaging. Kratom’s serious health risks include risks of abuse, dependence, addiction, overdose, and death.! Scientific literature has documented serious concerns regarding the toxicity of kratom in multiple organ systems. Consumption of kratom can lead to many adverse health impacts, including respiratory depression, nervousness, agitation, aggression, sleeplessness, hallucinations, delusions, tremors, loss of libido, constipation, skin hyperpigmentation, nausea, vomiting, and severe withdrawal signs and systems.” Effective treatments for kratom addiction and overdose have not been fully developed by the medical community. 24. Over the past ten years, reports of kratom poisonings and overdose deaths have risen dramatically throughout the country. 25. Kratom is already illegal in several states and cities, and it is not approved for medical purposes.
